source: Original KaiSip study notes, organized by The IIA's CIA Part 2 syllabus effective 2025. KaiSip is an independent study aid, not affiliated with or endorsed by The IIA.
overview: Section A is half of Part 2 and covers everything before fieldwork: setting objectives and scope, choosing criteria, recognizing the activity's business, IT and finance risks, picking an approach, completing the engagement risk assessment, writing the work program and sizing resources. Throughout, the internal auditor plans, the chief audit executive or a delegated engagement supervisor approves, and management owns the activity under review.
analogy: Planning an engagement is like a surveyor preparing to inspect a bridge. Before climbing anything, the surveyor reads the design, the traffic data and past reports, decides which spans to check and against which code, picks the instruments and the team, and has the inspection plan signed off by the chief engineer. If the owner bars access to a span, the surveyor does not quietly skip it: it goes on the record and up the chain. The owner, not the surveyor, repairs the bridge.

topics.overview: This topic covers how internal auditors decide what an engagement will achieve and what it will cover: the inputs to objectives, the boundaries of the scope, Topical Requirements, scope limitations, stakeholder requests and changes made along the way. Every later planning step rests on it.
can_do: Determine objectives from strategy, regulation, risk appetite, earlier reports and the assurance or advisory choice
Apply a Topical Requirement to a scope, recording each exclusion with its reason
Identify a scope limitation during planning and say who acts on it next
Evaluate a stakeholder request or a change during fieldwork and decide what it needs

subtopics.name: Inputs to Engagement Objectives
subtopics.definition: Engagement objectives state what an engagement sets out to achieve and why; internal auditors build them from the organization's direction, its rules and what is already known.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Objectives steer everything after them: the scope, the criteria, the work program and the conclusion. Objectives built on the wrong inputs send the team to test what does not matter.
how_it_works: Must (Standard 13.3 Engagement Objectives and Scope): objectives state the engagement's purpose and its specific goals, including any goal a law or regulation requires.
Must: consider first whether the work gives assurance or advice, because stakeholders expect different things and the Standards ask different things of each.
Must gather (Standard 13.2): the strategy, objectives and risks touching the activity, risk tolerance if set, the plan's risk assessment, and the activity's governance, risk and control processes.
Should: also read earlier reports and workpapers, other assurance providers' results, policies and sector laws, and align objectives with the activity's and the organization's goals.
subtopics.example: Lerato, an internal auditor at a South African water utility, plans an assurance engagement on meter billing. Lerato reads the strategy, the regulator's billing accuracy rule, last year's report on customer refunds and the external auditor's letter, then drafts objectives that include the regulator's required accuracy test and sends them to the engagement supervisor.

review: Trace each objective to a risk in the engagement risk assessment
Compare the objectives with any goals that laws or regulations set
Inspect the planning memo for the assurance or advisory decision
evidence: Planning memo linking objectives to strategy, risks and criteria
Extracts from prior reports showing open issues carried into objectives
Dated sign-off of the objectives in the engagement file
audit_focus.recommend: Have the chief audit executive's methodology require a documented link from every engagement objective to an assessed risk.
audit_focus.decides: The chief audit executive, or a delegated supervisor, approves the objectives

subtopics.isaca_rule: Must: state the purpose and specific goals, legally required goals included, after deciding whether the work is assurance or advisory. Build objectives from strategy, risks, tolerance and the activity's processes, not from management's wishes.

exam_traps.trap: The management of the activity under review decides the objectives of an assurance engagement.
exam_traps.why: In assurance work internal auditors mainly set objectives and scope, with management's input, and the chief audit executive approves them. Setting them jointly is the advisory pattern.

exam_traps.trap: Objectives can wait until fieldwork shows where the problems are.
exam_traps.why: Objectives come out of planning and drive the scope, criteria and work program. They may change later with approval, but they are set before testing.

key_terms.definition: What an engagement is meant to establish: its overall aim and the particular results it must deliver.
A workpaper summarizing an engagement's objectives, scope, risks, criteria and approach for approval.

subtopics.name: Setting the Scope and Applying Topical Requirements
subtopics.definition: Engagement scope sets the boundaries of the work, what is in and what is out; a Topical Requirement adds a mandatory minimum when an assurance scope covers its topic.
subtopics.why_it_matters: A scope too narrow misses the risks the objectives target; one that silently skips a Topical Requirement breaks a mandatory rule quality assessments check.
how_it_works: Must (Standard 13.3): the scope sets boundaries such as the period, sites, processes, systems and units covered, and must be enough to reach every objective.
A Topical Requirement applies when its topic is a planned engagement's subject, comes up during an engagement, or is the subject of a request outside the plan.
Assurance on the topic must conform; for advisory work conformance is recommended. Each requirement is assessed for applicability, and every exclusion is documented with its reason.
The 2025 Application Guidance makes this risk-based: requirements outside the identified risk may be excluded, and coverage may be spread over several engagements if documented.
Each requirement reaches the exam on its own date: Cybersecurity is testable now, and the other three follow in 2027.
subtopics.example: Mateus, an internal auditor at a Brazilian logistics firm, scopes an assurance engagement on the online booking portal. Attacks on the portal are a significant risk, so Mateus assesses each requirement of the Cybersecurity Topical Requirement, keeps risk management and controls in scope, and records that governance was covered by last year's cyber engagement.

review: Test whether each objective could be met within the agreed boundaries
Inspect the applicability record for every requirement of each relevant Topical Requirement
Evaluate whether each exclusion rests on evidence rather than preference
evidence: Topical Requirement applicability matrix with reasons for exclusions
Approved scope statement naming periods, sites, processes and systems
audit_focus.recommend: Have the chief audit executive add a Topical Requirement applicability check to the engagement planning template.
audit_focus.decides: The chief audit executive, or a delegate, approves the scope

subtopics.isaca_rule: Must: the scope is enough for every objective. When assurance covers a Topical Requirement's topic, assess each requirement and document why any is excluded; management's preference is not a reason. Advisory work: conformance is recommended.

exam_traps.trap: A Topical Requirement can be skipped when management says the topic was reviewed recently.
exam_traps.why: Applicability is the internal auditor's documented judgment. Earlier coverage can justify an exclusion once assessed and recorded, never on management's word alone.

exam_traps.trap: Once a Topical Requirement applies, every one of its requirements must be tested in that engagement.
exam_traps.why: Requirements outside the identified risk can be excluded with a recorded reason; coverage can also span several engagements.

key_terms.definition: A mandatory baseline for assurance engagements on a named subject, such as cybersecurity; recommended for advisory work.
The documented check of each requirement in a Topical Requirement: it applies here, or it is excluded for a stated reason.

subtopics.name: Scope Limitations and Stakeholder Requests
subtopics.definition: A scope limitation is a condition, such as blocked access or short resources, that stops planned assurance work; stakeholder requests ask to add, drop or shorten work.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Spotting limitations and risky requests during planning protects the conclusion. An unnoticed limitation leads to a conclusion that claims more than the work supports.
how_it_works: Standard 13.3 counts resource constraints and restricted access to people, facilities, data and information as scope limitations in assurance work.
Must: discuss a limitation with management when it is identified, aiming to resolve it; if it stays unresolved, the chief audit executive elevates it to the board.
Should: judge whether a request to include or exclude items, or to cap the engagement's length, amounts to a scope limitation.
Record each request, who made it, the decision and its reason in the workpapers; an added item is a scope change that needs approval.
subtopics.example: Ji-woo, planning a procurement engagement at a Korean electronics maker, receives two requests. The purchasing director asks to leave out emergency purchases as rare; the chief financial officer asks to add supplier rebates. Ji-woo finds emergency purchases are a fifth of spending, records both requests and takes them to the engagement supervisor: the exclusion would be a scope limitation, the rebates a scope change.

review: Trace each stakeholder request to a recorded decision and reason
Compare excluded items with the significant risks in the risk assessment
Inspect board papers for limitations that management left unresolved
evidence: Request log naming requester, item, decision and approver
Minutes of meetings where management responded to the limitation
Escalation paper sent to the board, with its date
audit_focus.recommend: Have the chief audit executive's methodology require a request log and a scope limitation check for every exclusion request.
audit_focus.decides: The board decides how to respond once the matter reaches it

subtopics.isaca_rule: Must: discuss a scope limitation with management when found; if unresolved, the chief audit executive elevates it to the board. Should: treat requests to exclude items or shorten the work as possible limitations. Record each request and decision.

exam_traps.trap: Note the scope limitation in the workpapers and carry on with what can be tested.
exam_traps.why: Noting it is not enough: discuss it with management to resolve it; if it stays unresolved, the chief audit executive elevates it to the board.

exam_traps.trap: A senior manager's request to drop an area is a courtesy that can simply be granted.
exam_traps.why: A request to exclude items may be a scope limitation: judge it against the risks, record it, and get approval for any scope change.

key_terms.definition: A condition in an assurance engagement, such as restricted access, that prevents the planned work.
A request from the board, management or others to add, exclude or limit part of an engagement.

subtopics.memory_aid: Spot it, discuss it with management, then the chief audit executive elevates it.

subtopics.name: Changing Objectives and Scope During the Engagement
subtopics.definition: A change in objectives or scope is an approved adjustment, made during the engagement, when the work shows the original goals or boundaries no longer fit the risks.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Fieldwork often reveals risks planning missed. A team that cannot adjust leaves a significant risk untested; one that adjusts without approval or notice loses control and trust.
how_it_works: Must (Standard 13.3): internal auditors keep the flexibility to change objectives and scope when the work shows the need.
Must: each change to objectives or scope is approved (Standard 13.3), just as the originals were.
Must (Standard 13.1 Engagement Communication): communicate changes to objectives, scope and timing to management in a timely way.
Must (Standard 13.6): update the work program and have the change approved promptly; added analysis work also needs the chief audit executive's approval (Standard 14.2).
Guard against scope creep: add only what the objectives and the significant risks need, and record why.
subtopics.example: Halfway through a payroll engagement at a Canadian university, internal auditor Priya finds overtime approved in a new scheduling app the plan never covered. Priya proposes adding the app's approval controls, and two days, to the engagement supervisor. Once it is approved, Priya updates the work program and tells the payroll manager the new scope and finish date.

review: Compare the final scope with the approved scope and each documented change
Inspect each change for approval before the related testing began
Confirm management heard about each change and its new timing
evidence: Approved change records with dates and approvers
Revised work program showing added or dropped steps
Emails or minutes informing management of the changes
audit_focus.recommend: Have the chief audit executive add a change log, with approver and date, to every engagement file.
audit_focus.decides: The chief audit executive, or a delegated supervisor, approves each change

subtopics.isaca_rule: Must: change objectives and scope when the work shows the need, with the chief audit executive's or a delegate's approval, a promptly approved work program and timely word to management. Never widen or narrow the work quietly.

exam_traps.trap: The internal auditor may expand the scope on the spot and tell management in the final report.
exam_traps.why: Each change needs approval by the chief audit executive or a delegate, and timely communication to management, not a note at the end.

exam_traps.trap: Approved objectives are fixed, so a newly found significant risk waits for a future engagement.
exam_traps.why: Standard 13.3 requires flexibility to change objectives and scope when the work shows the need; the change is weighed and approved now.

key_terms.definition: Growth of an engagement's coverage beyond what its objectives and significant risks need, often without a clear decision.
The internal auditor who supervises an engagement: the chief audit executive, or a delegate for whom the chief audit executive stays accountable.

topics.overview: Criteria are the yardstick the condition is measured against. This topic covers where criteria come from, how to pick the most relevant ones, how to judge whether the criteria the organization has set are adequate, and what to do when they are not.
can_do: Determine the most relevant criteria for an activity from internal, external and authoritative sources
Judge whether a criteria set is relevant, specific, practical, aligned and able to support reliable comparison
Decide what to do when the organization's criteria are inadequate or missing

subtopics.name: Where Criteria Come From
subtopics.definition: Evaluation criteria describe the desired state of the activity under review, the standard its actual condition is compared with, drawn from inside or outside the organization.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Without a fitting yardstick there is no finding and no conclusion. Criteria that miss the objectives produce findings management can fairly reject.
how_it_works: Must (Standard 13.4 Evaluation Criteria): identify the most relevant criteria for the parts of the activity the objectives and scope cover.
Internal sources: policies, procedures, key performance indicators and targets. External sources: laws, regulations and contracts.
Also usable in the right setting: authoritative frameworks and industry benchmarks, established practice, what a control's design implies, and procedures nobody wrote down.
Must (Standard 13.2): identify the criteria management uses to measure whether the activity meets its objectives; they are the first candidates.
A Topical Requirement gives baseline criteria for assurance on its topic; where a law or regulation is stricter, the stricter rule should guide the scope.
subtopics.example: Aroha, an internal auditor at a New Zealand regional council, plans an engagement on road maintenance contracts. Aroha lists possible criteria: the contract's response times, the council's procurement policy, the transport agency's safety rule and the council's own repair target. Aroha keeps the contract terms and the safety rule for the objective on contractor performance and notes which objective each criterion serves.

review: Trace each objective in the work program to its named criteria
Compare chosen criteria with the measures management uses for the activity
Inspect the source and version of each external criterion used
evidence: Criteria sheet listing each source, its owner and the objective served
Copies of the policy, contract or regulation version in force
audit_focus.recommend: Have the chief audit executive's methodology require a criteria sheet, linked to objectives, in every assurance planning file.

subtopics.isaca_rule: Must: identify the most relevant criteria for what the objectives and scope cover, starting from the measures management uses. Criteria can be internal, external or authoritative practice. For advisory work they may not be needed.

exam_traps.trap: Industry best practice is always the strongest criterion.
exam_traps.why: Relevance to the objectives and the activity decides. A benchmark from another setting may fit poorly, and adequate criteria set by the board and senior management must be used.

exam_traps.trap: Only written policies can serve as criteria.
exam_traps.why: Laws, contracts, targets, frameworks, established practice, a control's design and even undocumented procedures can be adequate criteria.

key_terms.definition: The yardstick for an engagement: what the activity should look like, taken from policy, law, contracts or good practice.
What the internal auditors actually found: the existing state of the activity.
Recognized outside guidance, such as a framework, a professional standard or an industry benchmark, used as a yardstick.

subtopics.name: Judging Whether Criteria Are Adequate
subtopics.definition: Adequate criteria are relevant to the objectives, consistent with the organization's and the activity's goals, specific, practical and able to give reliable comparisons.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Criteria decide what counts as a gap and how much it matters. Inadequate ones produce findings that are wrong, trivial or unprovable, and conclusions nobody can rely on.
how_it_works: Must (Standard 13.4): assess how far the board and senior management have set adequate criteria for the activity's objectives; if they are adequate, use them.
Must: if they are inadequate, work out appropriate criteria by discussing them with senior management, the board or both.
The considerations describe adequate criteria as relevant, aligned with objectives and giving reliable comparisons, and say criteria should be specific and practical.
Should: check whether the organization has defined its risk tolerance, materiality thresholds and a satisfactory level of control, such as 98 percent of payments approved.
May: suggest better criteria for the engagement, help management set them, or ask an expert; suggesting is not the same as replacing adequate criteria.

rows.label: Must
cells: Use them for the evaluation
Work out suitable criteria by discussing them with senior management, the board or both

rows.label: May
cells: Suggest better criteria for the engagement
Recommend management adopt the criteria identified; assist, or seek an expert's input

rows.label: Possible outcome
cells: Assurance against the existing criteria
The discussion may lead to advisory work instead

subtopics.example: Kofi audits drug-dispensing records at a Ghanaian hospital group. The pharmacy policy only says records must be accurate. Kofi judges this too vague to measure, so Kofi discusses criteria with the chief medical officer and the chief financial officer, who agree on a stock-count variance limit and a same-day recording rule. Kofi documents the agreed criteria and informs the pharmacy manager.

review: Evaluate each criterion against the objective it serves before testing
Compare management's measures with the stated tolerance and thresholds
Inspect the record of any discussion that replaced inadequate criteria
evidence: Minuted or written agreement on the criteria to be used
Policies or targets showing thresholds and the satisfactory level of control
audit_focus.recommend: Ask management to document measurable criteria, with thresholds, for the activity's key objectives.

subtopics.isaca_rule: Must: use adequate criteria the board and senior management have set; if they are inadequate, identify appropriate criteria by discussing them with senior management, the board or both. The considerations call adequate criteria relevant, aligned and comparable. May: suggest better ones.

exam_traps.trap: Adequate criteria set by the board and senior management can be swapped for the internal auditor's preferred standard.
exam_traps.why: If they are adequate, the internal auditor must use them. Better criteria may be suggested, not imposed.

exam_traps.trap: Criteria must be used simply because management set them.
exam_traps.why: Only adequate criteria must be used; inadequate ones give way to criteria worked out with the board, senior management or both.

key_terms.definition: The share of transactions or controls that must work as intended for a control process to count as acceptable.
The size of error or loss above which the organization treats a matter as significant for a unit or process.

subtopics.name: Criteria in Practice: Timing, Agreement and Gaps
subtopics.definition: Settling criteria in practice means fixing them in the work program before testing, telling management which ones will be used, and handling criteria that are missing.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Criteria picked after the results are known look like a verdict in search of a rule. Agreed, documented criteria prevent disputes about findings later.
how_it_works: Must (Standard 13.6): the work program names the criteria for each objective, so they are set before the work program is approved and testing begins.
Should: inform the management of the activity of the criteria and document the agreed set, so it is not misread or challenged later.
May: where criteria are inadequate or missing, recommend that management adopt the criteria the internal auditors identified.
May: a discussion about missing criteria can lead to advisory work instead of assurance.
Should: research recommended practice and compare management's criteria with other organizations'; a comparison informs judgment and does not override adequate criteria.
A new or changed objective needs its own criteria, approved with the revised work program.
subtopics.example: Before fieldwork on a Moroccan airline's fuel purchasing, internal auditor Youssef finds no written limit on hedging losses. Rather than test first and choose a limit later, Youssef proposes criteria based on the board's approved risk tolerance, shares them with the treasury manager, and records the agreement in the workpapers before the work program goes for approval.

review: Compare the date criteria were agreed with the date testing began
Inspect the work program for criteria named against every objective
Trace any criterion changed after testing to an approved change
evidence: Dated work program approval showing criteria for each objective
Email or minutes informing management of the criteria to be used
audit_focus.recommend: Have the chief audit executive require criteria to be agreed and documented before any work program is approved.
audit_focus.decides: The chief audit executive, or a delegate, approves the work program before testing

subtopics.isaca_rule: Set criteria before testing: the work program must name them for each objective. Should: tell management which criteria will be used and document the agreed set. May: when criteria are missing, recommend that management adopt them, or offer advisory work.

exam_traps.trap: Test first, then choose the criteria that best explain the exceptions found.
exam_traps.why: Criteria come before testing, and the work program names them for each objective. Criteria picked to fit the results look biased and invite challenge.

exam_traps.trap: Every advisory engagement needs formal evaluation criteria.
exam_traps.why: For advisory services, identifying criteria may not be needed, depending on the agreement with the relevant stakeholders.

key_terms.definition: A comparison point from another unit or organization; it informs a judgment but is not automatically a criterion.
Criteria shared with management and recorded before testing, so findings are measured against a known yardstick.

topics.topic_name: Planning around key risks and controls
topics.overview: Planning draws on business knowledge at recognize level: the activity's strategy and measures, cybersecurity and IT controls, readiness for disruption, finance basics, and the key risks of common processes and systems, with the Topical Requirements as a baseline. The aim is to spot the risk and the kind of control, not to configure or calculate.
can_do: Plan an engagement around the activity's strategic objectives and the measures management uses
Recognize cyber, IT, privacy and data security risks and the controls that commonly address them
Recognize continuity, recovery and resilience ideas that shape an engagement's risks
Recognize finance terms and the main risks of common business processes and systems

subtopics.name: Strategy, Performance Measures and Topical Requirements in Planning
subtopics.definition: Planning around strategy means starting from what the activity is trying to achieve, how its risks are managed and how management measures and manages its performance.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Risks matter because they threaten objectives. Starting from strategy and measures aims the engagement at what leaders care about, not at what is easiest to test.
how_it_works: Must (Standard 13.2): learn the strategy, objectives and risks that bear on the activity, and the criteria management uses to judge progress.
Look for the chain: a strategic objective, the risks to it, then the performance measures and targets that show whether it is on track.
Performance measures such as key performance indicators (KPIs) are often usable criteria; performance management is whether management reviews them and acts.
A measure that rewards one result can push risk elsewhere, for example a sales target that weakens credit checks; planning looks for that link.
A Topical Requirement in scope sets the minimum: map its governance, risk management and controls requirements to the risk assessment, criteria and work program steps.
subtopics.example: A Mexican bank's strategy is to double small-business lending in two years, tracked by loan volume. Planning an engagement on lending, internal auditor Valeria notes that volume is the only measure and that loan officers' bonuses depend on it. Valeria adds credit quality risk to the engagement risk assessment and plans to ask whether management tracks default rates by officer.

review: Trace each engagement objective to a strategic objective of the activity
Map each key risk to a measure that would reveal it
Sample performance reports for follow-up on missed targets
evidence: Strategy and business plan for the activity under review
Performance reports with targets, results and management's responses
audit_focus.recommend: Ask management to add measures that track the main risks to each strategic objective, not only output.
audit_focus.decides: Management sets the activity's measures; the board oversees strategy

subtopics.isaca_rule: Plan from the activity's objectives outward: strategy, the risks to it and the measures management uses. Must: gather them in planning (Standard 13.2). A Topical Requirement in scope is the minimum baseline, mapped into the work program.

exam_traps.trap: Planning starts from the list of controls management provides.
exam_traps.why: Planning starts from objectives and risks. Controls are judged by whether they manage the risks to the activity's objectives.

exam_traps.trap: A measure that is on target proves the risks are managed.
exam_traps.why: Targets show results, not risk. A measure can be met while risk builds elsewhere, so planning looks at how measures and risks connect.

key_terms.definition: A high-level goal an organization or activity sets in order to carry out its strategy.
A measure management uses to track progress toward an objective, such as on-time delivery.
How management sets targets, reviews results and acts on them.

subtopics.name: Cybersecurity, IT Controls and Data Protection
subtopics.definition: Cybersecurity protects systems, networks and data from attack and misuse; it is part of information security, which keeps information confidential, accurate and available.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Most processes run on technology, so cyber and IT weaknesses can defeat business controls; the Cybersecurity Topical Requirement sets a mandatory baseline and is testable now.
how_it_works: The Cybersecurity Topical Requirement says what internal auditors must assess: cyber governance, risk management (incident response and recovery included) and controls.
Controls it names include user access, configuration, patching, encryption, network segmentation, firewalls, endpoint and email security, and secure development.
It also expects management to monitor emerging threats continuously, such as those from artificial intelligence.
In common usage, IT general controls cover the whole IT environment (access, change, operations); application controls sit inside one system, such as input checks.
An IT control framework, such as NIST's, gives common language and coverage and can be mapped to the requirement; adopting one does not prove controls work.
Data protection starts with knowing what data is held, where, who can reach it and why; personal data brings privacy law into scope.
subtopics.example: Planning an engagement on online grocery orders for a Polish supermarket chain, internal auditor Kasia sees customer addresses and payment details passing through a vendor's platform. Kasia assesses the Cybersecurity Topical Requirement for applicability, plans to review the vendor's assurance report and the chain's access controls, and records that governance was covered by this year's cyber engagement.

review: Inspect the applicability record against each Cybersecurity Topical Requirement section
Compare system user lists with current staff and their roles
Inspect vendor assurance reports for scope, period and exceptions
evidence: System-generated user access listings with last review dates
Vendor service organization control (SOC) reports covering the period
Patch and vulnerability reports from security tools
audit_focus.recommend: Ask the chief information security officer to report access review and patching exceptions to management each quarter.
audit_focus.decides: Management owns cyber controls; the board oversees the cyber strategy

subtopics.isaca_rule: Recognize the risk and the kind of control; do not configure it. Must: for cyber assurance, assess the Topical Requirement's governance, risk management and controls requirements and document exclusions. Adopting a framework does not prove controls work.

exam_traps.trap: A periodic review of who can access the payroll system is an application control.
exam_traps.why: In common usage, managing system access is an IT general control; application controls sit inside one system, such as input checks.

exam_traps.trap: The organization follows a recognized IT control framework, so its cyber controls are effective.
exam_traps.why: A framework gives structure and language; whether controls are designed and working still has to be assessed.

key_terms.definition: Common-usage term for controls over the whole IT environment, such as access, change and operations, that every system relies on.
Common-usage term for controls built into one system, such as input checks and automatic matching.

subtopics.name: Continuity, Recovery and Resilience Readiness
subtopics.definition: Readiness for disruption is an organization's ability to keep critical services going and recover after a crisis, through continuity plans, recovery plans, incident response and tests.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Disruption is when untested plans fail. Recognizing whether recovery has been proven, not just written down, shows where an engagement's real risk sits.
how_it_works: A business continuity plan keeps critical work going in a disaster; a disaster recovery plan restores IT systems, data and operations afterward.
In common usage, a business impact analysis ranks activities by the cost of their disruption; the resilience user guide bases recovery teams and priorities on one.
Incident response covers detection, prioritization, containment, recovery and a post-incident review whose lessons feed future planning.
Completed backups prove little until data is restored; the resilience user guide links recovery objectives to restore testing.
The resilience requirement has auditors assess whether plans are tested, for example in tabletop rehearsals, and results reported to the board and senior management.
The Organizational Resilience Topical Requirement takes effect in April 2027 and is expected on the exam from October 2027.
subtopics.example: At a Thai hospital, the IT manager reports that nightly backups of patient records always complete. Planning a continuity engagement, internal auditor Somchai asks when data was last restored and how long it took. No restore has been tried in two years, so Somchai rates recovery as a significant risk and plans to review the recovery plan and its tests.

review: Inspect restore test results against the recovery time objective
Compare the systems restored first with the services ranked most critical
Trace issues from the last tabletop exercise to completed actions
evidence: Restore test logs with dates, systems and times achieved
Business impact analysis ranking critical services
Exercise reports and the action tracker that followed
audit_focus.recommend: Ask management to schedule restore tests for critical systems and report results against recovery objectives.
audit_focus.decides: Management owns the plans; the board receives test results

subtopics.isaca_rule: Written plans and completed backups do not prove readiness. Recognize whether continuity and recovery are prioritized by impact, tested and reported upward; management owns the plans and internal auditors assess them.

exam_traps.trap: Nightly backups that complete successfully show the organization can recover.
exam_traps.why: A backup that has never been restored is unproven. Readiness is shown by restore tests measured against the recovery objectives.

exam_traps.trap: Continuity planning is an IT matter only.
exam_traps.why: Continuity covers people, sites, suppliers and money as well as systems.

key_terms.definition: Common-usage term for a study of which activities matter most and what their disruption would cost over time.
In common usage, how quickly a system or service must be back after a disruption.
In common usage, how much recent data, measured in time, the organization can afford to lose.

subtopics.name: Finance Basics and Business Process Risks
subtopics.definition: Recognize-level business knowledge means knowing the main financial terms and the key risks of common processes well enough to spot what an engagement must cover.
subtopics.why_it_matters: An internal auditor who cannot tell an asset from a liability, or see why ordering and paying are kept apart, misses the risks that matter during planning.
how_it_works: The syllabus asks for recognition: name the concept and its typical risk, not compute or design. The glosses here are common usage, not keyed rules.
For assets, ask whether they exist, are protected and are valued properly; safeguarding assets is one aim of control (Standard 13.3, considerations).
For liabilities, ask whether all are recorded and paid on time; for capital and investments, whether they are authorized and valued properly.
Purchase to payment: ordering, receiving and paying are commonly kept apart and matched, so no one person can create and pay a false invoice.
In an enterprise resource planning (ERP) system, user roles decide who can do what, so access rights carry the risk of conflicting duties.
Third parties stay the organization's accountability; the Third-Party Topical Requirement (on the exam from March 2027) follows selection, contracting, onboarding, monitoring and exit.

rows.label: Current assets
cells: Cash and items expected to become cash or be used up within about a year, such as receivables and inventory
Do they exist, can they be collected or sold, and are they safe?

rows.label: Fixed assets
cells: Long-lived items used in the business, such as buildings, vehicles and equipment
Are they recorded, protected, and written down when worn or impaired?

rows.label: Short-term liabilities
cells: Amounts due within about a year, such as supplier invoices and wages owed
Is everything owed recorded and paid on time?

rows.label: Long-term liabilities
cells: Obligations due later, such as long loans or leases
Are terms and loan conditions met and reported?

rows.label: Capital and investments
cells: Owners' funding, and holdings bought to earn a return
Are they authorized, valued properly and within policy?

types.meaning: Risk of fictitious suppliers and duplicate or unapproved payments; ordering, receiving and paying are separated and matched.
Risk of loss, obsolete stock and failure of a single supplier; counts, minimum stock levels and alternative suppliers help.
Risk of lost or unrecorded equipment, IT assets included; an inventory tracks assets from purchase to disposal.
Risk of breaching laws, regulations or contracts; named owners, monitoring and reporting of breaches help.
Customer relationship management (CRM) systems hold personal data, ERP runs transactions, and governance, risk and compliance (GRC) systems hold risk records; access and accuracy matter.

subtopics.example: Planning an engagement on spare-parts purchasing at a Chilean copper mine, internal auditor Diego learns that one buyer can create suppliers, raise orders and release payments in the ERP system. Diego recognizes a high risk of payments to fictitious suppliers, notes stock held well above planned levels, and plans tests of supplier set-up, access rights and slow-moving inventory.

review: Compare ERP user roles with incompatible duties across purchase to payment
Trace a sample of payments to orders and receiving records
Inspect the third-party listing for completeness and risk ratings
evidence: System-generated role and access reports from the ERP system
Supplier master file change log with approver names
audit_focus.recommend: Ask the procurement and finance managers to remove conflicting access and require independent approval of supplier changes.
audit_focus.decides: Process owners decide how duties are split and accept any residual risk

subtopics.isaca_rule: Recognize, do not compute: name the asset, liability or process, its typical risk and the kind of control expected. Separated ordering, receiving and paying, and sound access rights in systems, are what planning looks for. Management owns the process.

exam_traps.trap: One approval on each payment makes the purchasing process safe.
exam_traps.why: In common practice ordering, receiving and paying are separated and matched. A single approval does not stop one person creating a supplier and paying it.

key_terms.definition: Common control practice of matching the purchase order, the receiving record and the supplier invoice before paying.
Dividing a transaction's key steps among different people so that no one can make and hide an error or fraud alone.

topics.overview: An engagement can be run in different ways: traditional, agile, integrated or remote. This topic covers what each offers, how to choose by objectives, risk and resources, and the project management ideas that keep an engagement on time and on budget. The Standards' musts apply whatever the approach.
can_do: Evaluate traditional, agile, integrated and remote ways of working for a given engagement
Determine which approach fits the objectives, risks, deadline and resources
Describe how scope, schedule, time budget and staffing are run like a project

subtopics.name: Traditional, Agile, Integrated and Remote Approaches
subtopics.definition: An engagement approach is the way the work is organized and delivered: in fixed stages, in short repeated cycles, across several disciplines at once, or from a distance.
subtopics.why_it_matters: The approach changes speed, cost and how often management sees results, but never the Standards. A newer approach is not permission to skip a requirement.
how_it_works: Every approach keeps the musts: documented objectives and scope, criteria, an approved work program, sufficient evidence, supervision and documentation.
Domain V of the Standards says engagement steps can overlap and repeat; agile work makes that visible, and each change to the work program is still approved.
Remote work does not lower the evidence bar: information must still be relevant, reliable and sufficient, so plan how to obtain it first-hand.
Integration needs the right mix of skills on one team, or specialists working to the same objectives under the same supervision.

types.meaning: Planning, fieldwork and reporting in sequence, with results mostly at the end. Predictable, but issues surface late.
Short cycles of planning, testing and feedback, with priorities adjusted as results arrive. Suits fast-changing areas; needs frequent contact.
One engagement brings together the disciplines the objectives need, such as process, IT and finance, instead of separate audits.
Work done away from the site through system access, video and shared files. Saves travel; observation and inspection get harder.

subtopics.example: Rangi leads an engagement on a new mobile payments app at an Australian credit union that releases updates every two weeks. Rangi proposes an agile approach: two-week testing cycles, an IT specialist on the team and a short results meeting with the product owner after each cycle. The engagement supervisor approves the work program for the first cycle, and each revision before it runs.

review: Compare the chosen approach with the objectives, risks and deadline
Confirm no cycle's testing started before its plan was approved
Sample remote evidence for its source, date and how it was obtained
evidence: Planning memo explaining why the approach was chosen
Approved work program versions for each cycle or stage
audit_focus.recommend: Have the chief audit executive's methodology state when each approach may be used and what each must still document.
audit_focus.decides: The chief audit executive, or a delegate, approves the work program

subtopics.isaca_rule: Pick the approach that serves the objectives, risks and resources, then keep every must: approved objectives, scope and work program, relevant, reliable and sufficient evidence, supervision and documentation. Agile changes timing and remote changes location; neither lowers the bar.

exam_traps.trap: Agile auditing means skipping a formal work program to move faster.
exam_traps.why: The work program must still be documented and approved before it is carried out, and promptly after changes; agile work approves it cycle by cycle.

exam_traps.trap: An integrated engagement is simply another name for an IT audit.
exam_traps.why: Integration brings the disciplines an objective needs, such as process, finance and IT, into one engagement.

key_terms.definition: How an engagement's work is organized and delivered, chosen to fit its objectives, risks and resources.
The chief audit executive's documented way of working, which internal auditors follow.

subtopics.name: Choosing the Approach That Fits
subtopics.definition: Choosing an approach means weighing the engagement's objectives, risks, complexity, deadline, stakeholders and resources, then picking the way of working that serves them best.
subtopics.why_it_matters: A choice made out of habit wastes effort or misses risk. Matching the approach to the job lets the team deliver reliable results when stakeholders need them.
how_it_works: Start from the objectives and the significant risks: what must be shown, to whom and by when.
Must (Standard 13.5 Engagement Resources): consider the engagement's nature and complexity, its time frame, and whether money, people and technology are enough.
Should: weigh constraints such as hours budgeted, timing, travel and work in several languages (Standard 13.5, considerations).
Follow the chief audit executive's methodologies, which set how engagements are performed (Standard 9.3 Methodologies).
Where a risk needs physical inspection or observation, plan a site visit even within a remote approach; first-hand evidence is more reliable.

rows.label: Fast-changing subject, early results wanted
cells: Agile
Approval of each work program revision

rows.label: Stable process, fixed reporting date
cells: Traditional
Issues surfacing late

rows.label: Risks spanning process, IT and finance
cells: Integrated
The right mix of skills and one set of criteria

rows.label: Scattered sites, data held centrally
cells: Remote
Risks that still need inspection on site

subtopics.example: Amara must review cash handling at forty small branches of a Nigerian microfinance bank within six weeks. Transaction data sits in one central system, but cash counts need someone on site. Amara plans a remote analysis of every branch's data to rank them, then surprise cash counts at the eight highest-risk branches, and explains the choice to the engagement supervisor.

review: Evaluate whether the planning memo ties the approach to objectives and risks
Compare budgeted hours and dates with what the approach demands
Inspect evidence plans for risks that need work on site
evidence: Planning memo with the approach and its reasons
Time and cost budget for the engagement
audit_focus.recommend: Have the chief audit executive's methodology require a documented reason for the approach chosen in each engagement.

subtopics.isaca_rule: Choose by objectives, risk and resources, not by habit or novelty. Must: weigh nature, complexity, time frame and resources (Standard 13.5). Keep evidence first-hand where the risk needs it, whatever the approach.

exam_traps.trap: Use last year's approach so the results are comparable.
exam_traps.why: Comparability is one factor. The approach must fit this engagement's objectives, risks, deadline and resources.

exam_traps.trap: Working remotely justifies accepting scanned copies in place of the inspection the risk needs.
exam_traps.why: Evidence must still be relevant, reliable and sufficient. If the risk needs inspection or observation, plan it, or treat the gap as a limit on the work.

key_terms.definition: What the engagement examines and how hard it is, which drive the skills, time and methods it needs.
A limit on how the work can be done, such as hours, timing, travel or language.

subtopics.name: Project Management in an Engagement
subtopics.definition: Project management in an engagement means running it like a project: a defined scope, a schedule, a time budget, assigned people, progress tracking and controlled changes.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Engagements that drift miss reporting dates and overrun budgets, and stakeholders stop trusting the function. The IIA's Competency Framework lists project management among internal auditors' professional skills.
how_it_works: Scope and deliverables: the approved objectives and scope, and the final communication stakeholders expect.
Schedule and time budget: Standard 13.3's considerations include setting the timeline; the supervisor assigns staff by the work program's steps and the time each needs.
People: Standard 13.6 Work Program requires the work program to name the internal auditor assigned to each task.
Tracking: the supervisor checks that the work program is completed (Standard 12.3); comparing actual with budgeted time can improve later planning.
Change control: changes to objectives, scope or the work program are approved and communicated, like changes to any project baseline.
Communication: agree with management at the start how often updates will come and who receives the final communication (Standard 13.1, considerations).
subtopics.example: Sofia supervises a six-week inventory engagement at an Italian fashion house. Sofia splits the work program into tasks, each with hours and an owner, sets weekly check-ins with the warehouse director and tracks hours used against the budget. When stock counts take longer than planned in week three, Sofia raises the overrun with the chief audit executive instead of dropping planned steps.

review: Compare budgeted and actual hours by task at engagement close
Inspect the work program for an owner and target date per task
Trace each schedule slip to a documented decision
evidence: Timesheets showing hours charged to each task
Status reports or meeting notes shared with management
audit_focus.recommend: Have the chief audit executive track budget-to-actual hours across engagements and use the results in future planning.
audit_focus.decides: The chief audit executive decides on extra time or staff

subtopics.isaca_rule: Treat an engagement as a project with an approved scope, a schedule, a time budget, named owners and controlled changes. Must: name the auditor for each task (Standard 13.6). Overruns go to the chief audit executive, not into quietly dropped steps.

exam_traps.trap: When fieldwork runs late, cut the lowest-risk steps without telling anyone.
exam_traps.why: Dropping planned steps changes the work program, and perhaps the scope; both need approval, and resource problems go to the chief audit executive.

key_terms.definition: The hours planned for each task, used to schedule staff and track progress.
A planned point in the schedule, such as the end of fieldwork, used to check progress.
Comparing the hours used with the hours planned, during or after the engagement.

topics.overview: The engagement risk assessment turns planning information into a ranked list of risks that drives the objectives, scope and tests. This topic covers completing it: the Topical Requirements' risk test, pervasive and emerging risks, the effect of change, structure and culture, and the methods used to rate and rank risks and controls.
can_do: Complete an engagement risk assessment that identifies, rates and ranks the activity's risks, fraud included
Recognize pervasive and emerging risks and how change, structure and culture shift them
Determine suitable methods and yardsticks to rank risks and pick the controls worth testing
Apply the risk-based test that decides which parts of a Topical Requirement apply

subtopics.name: Completing the Engagement Risk Assessment
subtopics.definition: Completing the engagement risk assessment means turning what was learned about the activity into a documented, ranked list of significant risks, fraud included, and their intended controls.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Everything after it rests on this step. A risk left off the list is never tested, and a wrongly ranked one takes time from the risks that matter.
how_it_works: Must (Standard 13.2 Engagement Risk Assessment): understand how the activity is meant to work, identify the potentially significant risks to its objectives, consider fraud, and prioritize by significance.
The plan's risk assessment is an input, never the engagement's own assessment (see 1C2.2).
Must: where past engagements identified the relevant risks, review and update that assessment; reusing it unchanged does not meet the requirement.
Should: consider management's input on objectives, risks and controls; a shared understanding helps, but the internal auditor judges significance.
Topical Requirement test (2025 Application Guidance): rate the topic's inherent risk by impact and likelihood; above the threshold tied to risk appetite, map it to the requirements that apply.
subtopics.example: Planning a second engagement on grant payments at a Kenyan development agency, internal auditor Wanjiru starts from the assessment done three years ago. Wanjiru updates it for a new online application portal, a cut in finance staff and a donor's alert about fake grantees. Wanjiru adds and ranks the new risks, fraud among them, and sends the updated assessment to the engagement supervisor.

review: Compare the assessment's date and inputs with changes since the last engagement
Confirm fraud risks were identified and ranked with the others
Trace each significant risk to an objective and a planned test
evidence: Dated engagement risk assessment with ratings and reasons
Notes of planning discussions with management and the supervisor
audit_focus.recommend: Have the chief audit executive's methodology require a dated review of any earlier engagement risk assessment before reuse.
audit_focus.decides: The chief audit executive, or a delegate, approves the resulting objectives and scope

subtopics.isaca_rule: Must: understand the activity, identify the significant risks to its objectives, consider fraud and rank them. An earlier engagement's assessment is reviewed and updated, never reused as is. The plan's assessment and management's views are inputs; the ranking is the internal auditor's.

exam_traps.trap: Last cycle's engagement risk assessment can be reused unchanged.
exam_traps.why: Where past engagements identified the risks, a review and update is enough, but it is required: changes since then may add or re-rank risks.

exam_traps.trap: Management's own risk register can replace the engagement risk assessment.
exam_traps.why: Management's assessment can help identify risks, but the internal auditor must assess and rank the activity's risks, judging significance independently.

key_terms.definition: The planning step that identifies and ranks the risks of the activity being examined.
In the Topical Requirements Application Guidance, the level of risk, tied to risk appetite, above which a topic counts as significant.

subtopics.name: Pervasive and Emerging Risks
subtopics.definition: Pervasive risks run through a whole activity, not one step, such as financial, operational, IT, cyber and regulatory risk; emerging risks are new or changing, with little history.
subtopics.why_it_matters: A risk assessment built step by step can miss risks that touch every step, and last year's data misses what is new.
how_it_works: Pervasive means present across the activity: a weak system or a new regulation touches every process that uses it or falls under it.
Standard 3.1's considerations name fraud as a pervasive risk, and Standard 13.2 requires fraud risk to be considered in every engagement risk assessment.
The Cybersecurity user guide expects cyber risk to be considered in planning, scoping and carrying out most assurance engagements, not only cyber ones.
Emerging risks include new technology such as artificial intelligence, new regulation, market shifts and slow-building pressures that are easy to overlook.
With little loss history, emerging risks are rated by judgment, scenarios and outside sources such as regulators, industry bodies and threat intelligence.
subtopics.example: Planning an engagement on the claims process at a Dutch health insurer, internal auditor Daan lists step-level risks such as duplicate claims. Daan then adds risks that cut across every step: weak change controls in the claims system, a national data law starting next year, and a plan to let an artificial intelligence tool approve small claims.

review: Compare the risk list with risks that span every process step
Inspect planning notes for regulatory and technology changes due soon
Evaluate whether new risks were rated low only for lack of losses
evidence: Regulatory change calendar or compliance team updates
Industry or threat reports used in rating
audit_focus.recommend: Ask management to add emerging risks, with owners and review dates, to the activity's risk register.
audit_focus.decides: Management owns the risk register and the responses to emerging risks

subtopics.isaca_rule: Look across the activity as well as along it: financial, operational, IT, cyber and regulatory risks touch every step, and fraud is considered in every engagement. Rate emerging risks by judgment and outside information; do not wait for losses.

exam_traps.trap: A risk with no losses to date can be rated low.
exam_traps.why: Emerging risks have little history. Their rating rests on judgment and outside information about likelihood and impact, not on past losses.

exam_traps.trap: IT risk belongs only in IT engagements.
exam_traps.why: Most processes run on systems, so IT and cyber risks are pervasive and are considered when planning engagements on business processes too.

key_terms.definition: A risk present across an activity or organization rather than in a single step, such as fraud or system failure.
A new or fast-changing risk with little history, whose likelihood and impact are still uncertain.
Information about current and likely attacks, used to anticipate cyber risk.

subtopics.name: Change, Structure and Culture as Risk Factors
subtopics.definition: Change, structure and culture are conditions around an activity, such as new people or systems, how decisions are spread and how people behave, that move its risks.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Controls are designed for a setting. When people, systems or structure change, or culture rewards the wrong things, working controls can quietly fail.
how_it_works: Change in people (turnover, reliance on one person), processes (new steps, outsourcing) or systems (new or migrated software) is a common reason risks rise.
Structure and work setting move where risk gathers and where review happens; the table shows what to ask for each.
May: use organizational charts and job descriptions to see who is responsible, then confirm it through interviews and walk-throughs (Standard 13.2, considerations).
Culture shapes the control environment beneath every process: tone at the top, incentives, accountability and whether people feel able to speak up.
The Organizational Behavior Topical Requirement covers these behavioral risks; it takes effect in December 2026 and is expected on the exam from June 2027.

rows.label: Centralized
cells: One system, team or leader, which can become a single point of failure
Is there backup, and independent review at the center?

rows.label: Decentralized
cells: Local practices and reliance on local leaders
Do policies apply everywhere, and do local issues reach head office?

rows.label: Flat structure
cells: Wide spans of control with fewer reviewers
Who reviews and approves, and is that person independent of the work?

rows.label: Traditional layers
cells: Many approval steps that can slow escalation
Do urgent issues and bad news travel up quickly?

rows.label: Remote or hybrid work
cells: Access, devices and supervision at a distance
How are work, access and approvals monitored?

subtopics.example: A Peruvian food exporter has moved its regional offices into one shared service center and removed a layer of supervisors. Planning an engagement on export documents, internal auditor Lucia notes a new system, staff new to the work and approvals now given by one team lead, so Lucia raises the rating for document errors and plans to test who reviews each shipment.

review: Compare charts and job descriptions with who actually approves
Inspect records of new systems, processes or staff during the period
Evaluate whether incentives reward behavior that works against controls
evidence: Organization charts before and after the change
Staff turnover and vacancy figures for the activity
Themes from employee surveys or speak-up channels
audit_focus.recommend: Ask management to reassess the activity's risks and controls whenever people, processes, systems or structure change significantly.
audit_focus.decides: Management owns the change and its controls; the board oversees culture

subtopics.isaca_rule: A control designed for yesterday's setting may not fit today's. Rate risk higher where people, processes, systems or structure have changed, or where culture rewards the wrong behavior, and confirm where decisions are really made.

exam_traps.trap: If the policy manual is unchanged, a reorganization does not affect the risk assessment.
exam_traps.why: Controls depend on who does the work and where; a new structure, system or team can leave a written control undone.

exam_traps.trap: Culture is a soft topic outside a process engagement's risk assessment.
exam_traps.why: Culture shapes the control environment beneath every process. Tone, incentives and willingness to speak up raise or lower risk in the activity under review.

key_terms.definition: Reliance on one person whose absence would stop or weaken a process or a control.
The observable choices people make at work and how they work with others; part of culture.

subtopics.name: Rating and Ranking Risks and Controls
subtopics.definition: Rating and ranking means scoring each identified risk, usually by impact and likelihood, then ordering the risks and their key controls so testing goes where it matters most.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Time is limited. A ranking built on evidence and the organization's own thresholds keeps the engagement on significant risks instead of easy tests.
how_it_works: Must (Standard 13.2): evaluate each risk's significance and prioritize. The considerations estimate it from impact, likelihood and possibly other factors, often on a heat map.
Use the organization's own yardsticks where they exist: risk appetite, risk tolerance and materiality thresholds for the unit or process.
Significance is relative: a risk small for the organization can be significant for the activity under review (Standard 4.2, considerations).
Rate inherent risk before counting controls, then judge the controls (definitions in 1C4.3).
May: for the most significant risks, assess control design first to decide which controls to test for operating effectiveness.
A risk and control matrix can record each risk, its control and type, cause, effect and residual risk.
subtopics.example: Internal auditor Farida plans an engagement on cash collection at an Egyptian toll-road operator. Farida scores six risks for impact and likelihood, setting the impact bands from the board's loss tolerance. Skimming at manual lanes scores highest, so Farida plans to judge the design of the lane cash controls first and test the sound ones in depth.

review: Compare risk ratings with the organization's stated thresholds and tolerance
Inspect whether inherent ratings were set before controls were counted
Trace the top-ranked risks to the most extensive planned tests
evidence: Heat map or rating sheet with defined scoring scales
Risk and control matrix with control types and design notes
audit_focus.recommend: Have the chief audit executive define common rating scales and require reasons for each engagement's top-ranked risks.
audit_focus.decides: The chief audit executive, or a delegate, approves the resulting work program

subtopics.isaca_rule: Rank by impact and likelihood against the organization's own thresholds, not by ease of testing. Rate inherent risk first, then weigh the controls. May: judge design for the most significant risks before testing operation.

exam_traps.trap: Put first the risks that are quickest to test, to show progress early.
exam_traps.why: Priority follows significance, judged by impact and likelihood. Easy tests on minor risks leave the significant ones under-tested.

exam_traps.trap: Score the risk after counting the controls and record it as inherent risk.
exam_traps.why: Inherent risk is rated before controls; counting them first hides how much the activity depends on controls that may fail.

key_terms.definition: A grid plotting risks by likelihood and impact so the most significant stand out.
A control that a significant risk mainly depends on, and so a candidate for testing.
A working table that lines up objectives, risks and the controls meant to manage them.

topics.overview: The work program turns planning into tasks. This topic covers procedures that judge control design, tests of effectiveness and efficiency, test methods for finance, IT, operations and cybersecurity, and how to judge whether a work program is good enough to approve.
can_do: Determine procedures that judge a control's design before its operation is tested
Identify tests of effectiveness and of efficiency, and tell the two apart
Evaluate whether a work program meets the Standards and is ready for approval
Identify test methods that suit finance, IT, operations or cybersecurity objectives

subtopics.name: Procedures to Judge Control Design
subtopics.definition: A design procedure asks whether a control, performed as intended, would manage its risk: acting at the right point, by the right person, with the right information and follow-up.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Testing how faithfully a badly designed control is performed wastes effort and gives false comfort. Design work also shows which key controls deserve operating tests.
how_it_works: Walk a transaction through the process to see where the control acts and what its performer actually sees.
Compare each control with its risk in the risk and control matrix: does it prevent or detect the event, and early enough?
Inspect the procedures, system settings and reports the control relies on, and ask what happens to exceptions.
May: judge design during planning, as a separate stage, or while testing operation; the considerations leave the timing to the engagement.
Should: document the design evaluation in the work program or a separate workpaper (Standard 13.6, considerations).
A design gap is already a potential finding; further work then sizes its effect instead of testing faithful performance.
subtopics.example: At a Vietnamese garment maker, the work program calls for testing a monthly review of overtime. Internal auditor Linh first walks through the review and finds the manager sees only total hours, not hours per worker, so excessive shifts cannot show up. Linh records a design gap and proposes to the engagement supervisor an analysis of overtime per worker in place of the planned sample.

review: Confirm each key control's design was judged before its sample was drawn
Trace design gaps to potential findings rather than operating tests
evidence: Screenshots or copies of the reports the performer relies on
Design evaluation workpaper linked to the risk and control matrix
audit_focus.recommend: Have the chief audit executive's methodology require a documented design evaluation before any operating test of a key control.
audit_focus.decides: Management owns the control and decides how to redesign it

subtopics.isaca_rule: Ask whether it would work before asking whether it was done. May: judge design at planning or alongside operating tests. Should: document it. A design gap is a potential finding, and testing faithful performance of a flawed control adds little assurance.

exam_traps.trap: Sample sixty instances first; the design can be judged from the results.
exam_traps.why: Perfect performance of a control that cannot catch the risk proves nothing. Judging design first shows whether operating tests are worth doing.

key_terms.definition: Whether a control, performed as written, would keep its risk at an acceptable level.
Following one transaction from start to finish to see how the process really works.

subtopics.name: Testing Effectiveness and Efficiency
subtopics.definition: Effectiveness tests show whether a control worked as designed over the period; efficiency tests show whether it costs no more time or money than the risk warrants.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Both questions are in the syllabus. Confusing them, or accepting a manager's word as proof, leads to conclusions the evidence cannot carry.
how_it_works: Effectiveness methods: inspect records of the control, reperform it, observe it, confirm results with an independent party, or analyze the full data population.
Inquiry on its own is weak: an answer from the control's performer is neither first-hand nor corroborated (Standard 14.1).
Should: when sampling, the work program records the method, population, sample size and whether results can be projected (Standard 13.6, considerations).
Draw samples from across the whole period, or test every item with data analysis software, which the considerations encourage.
Efficiency methods: compare a control's cost and time with the risk, look for duplicate controls over one risk, and spot manual steps a system could do.
A chance to improve efficiency is a legitimate potential finding (Standard 14.2, considerations).

rows.label: Question
cells: Did the control work, every time, over the period?
Is its cost in time and money proportionate to the risk?

rows.label: Typical methods
cells: Reperform, inspect, observe, confirm, analyze all the data
Time and cost the steps, map overlapping controls

rows.label: Typical potential finding
cells: Control skipped, or exceptions not followed up
Duplicate, excessive or slow controls

subtopics.example: Testing a three-signature approval of travel claims at a Swiss foundation, internal auditor Nora reperforms the approval on claims drawn from all twelve months and finds it always done. Nora also times the process: claims under 100 francs take three weeks and cost more to approve than they are worth. Nora records the control as effective but inefficient for small claims.

review: Inspect whether samples span the whole period under review
Inspect conclusions resting only on interviews for corroborating evidence
Evaluate whether efficiency work weighed cost against the risk managed
evidence: Reperformance results and exception lists
Data analysis scripts and full-population outputs
audit_focus.recommend: Ask management to remove or merge duplicate controls once the remaining control is shown to manage the risk.
audit_focus.decides: Management decides which controls to keep, merge or remove

subtopics.isaca_rule: Effectiveness asks whether the control worked; efficiency asks at what cost. Prove effectiveness with evidence beyond inquiry, drawn from across the period. Should: record sampling details in the work program.

exam_traps.trap: The process owner said in an interview that the control runs daily, so it is effective.
exam_traps.why: Inquiry alone comes from the person under review and is uncorroborated. Effectiveness needs evidence such as inspection, reperformance or data analysis.

exam_traps.trap: Testing one week in detail shows how the control worked all year.
exam_traps.why: A narrow window says little about the rest of the period. Sample across the period, or test the full population.

key_terms.definition: The internal auditor carrying out the control again to see whether it gives the right result.
How test items are chosen, from which population, how many, and whether the results can be projected.

subtopics.name: Judging Whether the Work Program Is Adequate
subtopics.definition: An adequate work program is the documented, approved plan of tasks that would achieve every engagement objective, built on the planning work and the engagement risk assessment.
subtopics.why_it_matters: The work program links planning to fieldwork. A gap here, such as a missing criterion or owner, becomes a gap in evidence and conclusions later.
how_it_works: Must (Standard 13.6): base it on the planning information, including the results of the engagement risk assessment where one was done.
Must: it identifies the criteria for each objective, the tasks, the methods and tools (analytical procedures included) and the internal auditor assigned to each task.
Must: it is reviewed and approved before it is carried out, and promptly after any change.
The considerations make the main approval test whether it achieves the objectives efficiently (Standard 12.3).
Should: leave room to record who did each step, when, and its review, and cross-reference the planning workpapers.
Should: for advisory work, develop it together with the stakeholders who asked for the service.
subtopics.example: Engagement supervisor Hamid reviews a draft work program for a Jordanian telecom's roaming revenue engagement. Every objective has tasks, but the revenue completeness objective names no criterion and two tasks have no assigned auditor. Hamid sends it back, and fieldwork waits until a corrected version is approved.

review: Compare the draft work program with the methodology's required elements
Compare the approval date with the date fieldwork began
Trace each significant risk to at least one task
evidence: Approved work program showing dates and approver
Approved change records for later revisions
audit_focus.recommend: Have the chief audit executive's methodology include a work program checklist that holds fieldwork until approval.
audit_focus.decides: The chief audit executive, or a delegated supervisor, approves it before fieldwork

subtopics.isaca_rule: Must: criteria, tasks, methods and tools, and an assigned auditor, built on planning; approved before it is carried out and promptly after changes. The considerations add the approval test: does it achieve the objectives efficiently?

exam_traps.trap: Fieldwork can start while the work program waits for approval, as long as it is approved before the report.
exam_traps.why: The chief audit executive, or a delegate, must review and approve the work program before it is carried out.

exam_traps.trap: Once approved, the work program cannot change.
exam_traps.why: It changes when the work shows the need; each change is approved promptly, and added analysis needs the chief audit executive's approval.

key_terms.definition: The approved list of steps an engagement will perform to meet its objectives.
A dated initial or record showing who completed or reviewed a work program step.

subtopics.name: Test Methods by Subject Area
subtopics.definition: Test methods are the procedures chosen to gather evidence, and the usual mix differs by subject: accounting and finance, IT systems, business operations or cybersecurity.
subtopics.why_it_matters: A generalist internal auditor is expected to recognize which method suits which subject. Choosing a method because it is familiar, not because it answers the objective, weakens the evidence.
how_it_works: Accounting and finance: reconcile balances, trace entries to source documents, confirm balances with outside parties, and compare results with budgets, earlier periods and ratios.
IT systems: extract data directly from systems, inspect user lists and settings, and review records of changes, working with system users and administrators.
Business operations: observe and walk through the process, compare nonfinancial data such as headcount with financial data such as payroll, and benchmark.
Cybersecurity: assess against the Topical Requirement, using access and patching reports, vendor assurance reports and the results of incident response tests.
Across subjects, prefer evidence the internal auditor obtains directly or from an independent source, and corroborate key points (Standard 14.1).
subtopics.example: Planning a fleet fuel engagement at a Saudi logistics company, internal auditor Reem matches a method to each objective: data analysis of every fuel card transaction against vehicle tank sizes, observation of refueling at two depots, and inspection of the fuel system's user list. Reem records each method and tool in the work program.

review: Compare each planned method with the objective and subject it serves
Inspect cyber steps against the Cybersecurity Topical Requirement's sections
Evaluate whether methods yield first-hand or independent evidence
evidence: Data extraction logs showing the source system and date
Confirmation replies received directly from outside parties
audit_focus.recommend: Have the chief audit executive keep test method guides for finance, IT, operations and cybersecurity engagements.

subtopics.isaca_rule: Match the method to the subject and the objective, not to habit. Data analysis, confirmation, reconciliation, observation and system inspection each suit different risks, and the work program must name the methods and tools.

exam_traps.trap: One method, such as interviews, can serve every subject area.
exam_traps.why: Different subjects need different evidence. Interviews build understanding, but finance, IT and cyber objectives usually need records, system data or independent confirmation.

key_terms.definition: Evidence obtained directly from an independent party, such as a bank or customer, about a balance or fact.
Comparisons of data, such as ratios, trends and budgets, used to spot unusual results.
An independent assurance report on a service provider's controls, which the organization using the service can review.

topics.topic_name: Resources and skills for the engagement
topics.overview: Every engagement needs enough of the right people, money and technology. This topic covers sizing them during planning and what to do when they fall short, from the internal auditor's seat: raise it with the chief audit executive, and never shrink the work quietly.
can_do: Determine the people, skills, money and technology an engagement needs
Evaluate what a shortfall means for the objectives, the scope and the conclusion
Decide who must hear about a shortfall and which options can close it

subtopics.name: People and Skills for the Engagement
subtopics.definition: Human resources for an engagement are the internal auditors and specialists assigned to it, chosen for the competencies, numbers and availability its tasks need.
subtopics.why_it_matters: An engagement staffed with the wrong skills produces evidence nobody can rely on. Competence is a personal must for each internal auditor and a collective one for the function.
how_it_works: Must (Standard 13.5): identify the types and quantity of resources needed, weighing the engagement's nature, complexity and time frame.
In practice the supervisor assigns people by the work program's steps and the time each needs, using what the chief audit executive knows of staff competencies.
Must (Standard 3.1 Competency): take on only work you have, or can obtain, the competencies for; supervised learning on the job counts.
How much supervision is needed depends on the auditors' experience and the engagement's complexity (Standard 12.3).
May: add skills through a guest auditor, an external service provider or another assurance provider (Standard 10.2, considerations).
A borrowed expert must be objective: someone from the activity under review cannot test their own area.
subtopics.example: An engagement on a Malaysian palm oil company's carbon credit sales needs carbon market knowledge no internal auditor has.
